fetched_contents.text: Financial Inclusion INVESTING IN FINANCIAL INCLUSION lp-heading-border-spacing-default lp-heading-top-spacing-default Access to affordable financial services — such as payments, credit, savings products, and insurance — is critical for poverty reduction and economic growth. In Emerging Markets and Developing Economies (EMDEs), 80 percent of the adults that saved could more easily cope with emergencies. Wide-spread adoption of digital payments by individuals and larger businesses could motivate formalization of smaller businesses. Global account ownership increased from 51 percent in 2011 to 76 percent in 2021. Despite such encouraging progress, more than a billion people around the world remain financially excluded. 65 percent of adults in the world’s low-income economies lack access to even the most basic transaction account. Half of adults in EMDEs cannot financially cope with an emergency. The gender gap, while narrowing, remains substantial in developing economies, particularly in Sub-Saharan Africa and the Middle East North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan. The large unmet need for credit from Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) in developing economies is estimated to be in the trillions of dollars. The average cost of sending money home is still high at around 6 percent. Low financial and digital literacy are also barriers. Digital financial services (DFS), enabled by fintech, are lowering costs, increasing speed, security, and transparency of transactions, enabling access for underserved sections. DFS addresses both supply side and demand side barriers. As of early 2020, there were over 850 million registered mobile money accounts across 90 countries, with $1.3 billion transacted per day. DFS lowers the cost of remittances and improves efficiency and integrity of government payments. Officially recorded remittance flows to EMDEs in 2022 were estimated to be $630 billion. While the benefits of financial services are well documented, DFS introduce risks to users and to the broader financial system, including predatory lending, data privacy concerns, unequal access to technology, and cyber-security and operational risks. Policy makers will need to ensure their policy frameworks remain “fit for purpose.” The World Bank Group is assisting EMDEs in responsibly harnessing DFS — working on DFS in over 50 countries through lending and advisory, investing in data sources, fostering risk capital, and IFC investments to accelerate adoption. fetched_contents.text: Measuring Digital Financial Inclusion in Emerging and Developing Economies: A New Index in: IMF Working Papers Volume 2021 Issue 090 (2021) Abstract Adoption of technology in the financial services industry (i.e. fintech) has been accelerating in recent years. To systematically and comprehensively assess the extent and progress over time in financial inclusion enabled by technology, we develop a novel digital financial inclusion index. This index is based on payments data covering 52 developing countries for 2014 and 2017, taking into account both access and usage dimentions of digital financial services (DFSs). This index is then combined with the traditional measures of financial inclusion in the literature and aggregated into an overall index of financial inlusion. There are two key findings: first, the adoption of fintech has been a key driver of financial inclusion. Second, there is wide variation across countries and regions, with the greatest progress recorded in Africa and Asia and the Pacific regions. This index should offer a useful analytical tool for researchers and policy makers. I. Introduction The rapid adoption of digital technology in finance offers a large potential to increase financial inclusion, namely, access to and usage of financial services by a wide section of the population. Digital financial services (DFSs), enabled by fintech (technological innovation in the financial sector), can help overcome the often-cited obstacles in accessing traditional financial services such as cost, geographical barriers, and information asymmetry. Recognizing this potential, the United Nations, Sustainable Development Goals include targets both on traditional and digital inclusion measures (Target 8.10). There are several anecdotal evidence, including country-based case studies (Jack and Suri, 2011; 2014; Tarazi and Breloff, 2010) and regional studies (Sy et. al., 2019; Berkmen et. al., 2019; Loukoianova et al, 2019, Lukonga, 2018, and Blancher et al., 2019), that show how fintech is increasing access to financial services, especially for those previously unbanked or underserved. Existing literature primarily focuses on financial inclusion facilitated by financial institutions such as banks, i.e. traditional financial inclusion. This is measured by indicators related to access to and/or usage of traditional financial services, such as the number of bank account per capita and ATM per capita, or combining these indicators into a composite index (Beck, Demirguc-Kunt and Martinez Peria, 2007, Honohan, 2008). Some recent studies have quantified the degree of digital financial inclusion by looking at relevant indicators, such as mobile money accounts and financial transactions using mobile phone (Sy et al., 2019; Loukoianova et al., 2019; Camara and Tuesta, 2017). However, these measures capture a single aspect of digital financial inclusion at a time, and do not present a comprehensive picture of combining multiple aspects including access and usage. This paper aims to fill this gap in the existing literature by incorporating both measures of access to and usage of DFSs into the measurement of financial inclusion. Methodological variables and controls used in fintech impact studies

Researchers in fintech impact studies typically distinguish fintech adoption from broader financial sector change by focusing on fintech-specific adoption metrics rather than generic financial-sector growth or penetration indicators. The evidence shows that fintech studies use digital financial inclusion indices and fintech-enabled access measures to capture the unique contribution of fintech, such as mobile money accounts, digital payments, app usage, and transaction volumes, while broader financial inclusion indicators remain important for comparison [N3-F4][N3-R1][N3-R5]. This distinction is important because fintech adoption can be a subset of broader financial-sector transformation, and studies need to isolate fintech effects from other financial development or regulatory changes.

Standard control variables in cross-country and panel studies are broad and include macroeconomic and institutional controls. The econometric evidence points to panel-data methods and instrumental variables (IV) as key methodological tools, with IV used to address endogeneity and identification problems. The World Bank working paper on policy research explicitly discusses instrumental variable approaches using cross-sectional and panel data, and another source notes the estimation of factor-augmented panel data models using observed measurements to proxy for unobserved factors or loadings [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R4]. Although the evidence does not list every possible control variable, the methodological literature implies that researchers commonly include variables such as GDP growth, inflation, interest rates, credit expansion, and possibly financial depth indicators as standard controls.

Researchers address endogeneity and identification in fintech studies by using instrumental variables and panel-data strategies. The evidence explicitly identifies IV as a method for treatment assignment where the instrument influences fintech adoption but not the outcome directly, and it also references double-filter instrumental variable estimation in panel data models with weakly exogenous variables [N4-R3][N4-R5]. This suggests that identification strategies in fintech studies are often designed to separate adoption from outcome and to account for reverse causality or omitted-variable bias. The evidence also points to the use of observed measurements as proxies for unobserved factors, which helps mitigate identification problems when direct data on adoption drivers are limited [N4-R2][N4-R4].

Variables used to proxy for omitted factors include institutional quality and technology readiness. The econometric evidence mentions observed measurements as proxies for unobserved factors or loadings, which can include institutional quality, regulatory environment, and technology readiness [N4-R2][N4-R4]. The contextual material from the fintech and digital finance literature also implies that researchers use fintech-specific adoption metrics such as mobile money accounts, financial transactions, app downloads, and transaction volumes as proxies for technology readiness and adoption intensity [N3-R1][N3-R5]. Together, these controls and proxies help researchers distinguish fintech effects from broader financial-sector or macroeconomic changes.

The official UNDP source defines the SDGs as covering poverty eradication, hunger, health, education, gender equality, and environmental sustainability, while emphasizing that the goals are designed to end poverty, hunger, AIDS, and discrimination against women and girls through improved health, education, and reduced inequality [N2-R1][N2-R3]. The evidence also shows that poverty is measured in terms of extreme poverty, multidimensional poverty, and access to basic needs, while employment and living standards are measured through income, poverty reduction, and access to services [N2-F2]. Specifically, the UNDP material states that extreme poverty fell below 10 percent globally, but 736 million people still lived on less than $1.90 a day, and 1.3 billion lived in multidimensional poverty [N2-F2].

For education and health outcomes, the evidence indicates that studies use indicators such as access to education, health services, and measures of malnutrition and undernourishment. The UNDP source highlights Goal 2 Zero Hunger and Goal 3 Good Health and Well-being, with undernourishment dropping by nearly half in the past two decades, while 821 million people were still chronically undernourished in 2017 [N2-F2]. It also notes that severe food insecurity and underweight among children remain major concerns, with over 90 million children under five dangerously underweight [N2-F2]. Education outcomes are indirectly operationalized through broader SDG language and poverty reduction goals, though the evidence does not provide a detailed enumeration of education-specific variables beyond SDG-aligned terminology.

Environmental sustainability and green finance outcomes are measured through carbon emissions, renewable energy, energy efficiency, and investment flows. The fintech and green finance source explicitly links fintech to green finance and sustainable development, stating that green finance aligns financial flows with sustainability objectives by supporting renewable energy, energy-efficient construction, and other environmentally advantageous activities [N5-R2]. It also notes that the study’s bibliometric analysis focuses on carbon emissions, renewable energy, green technology innovation, and fintech [N5-F3]. This indicates that environmental outcomes are often operationalized through proxies such as emissions, clean-energy investment, and innovation in green technology, rather than through a single direct environmental indicator.

SDG-aligned metrics are operationalized in studies linking fintech to sustainability by using composite indicators and proxy variables. The green finance source emphasizes the need to harmonize financial strategies with sustainability objectives and to use ESG-related variables and performance indicators [N5-F3]. It also notes that the study uses PRISMA and bibliometric analyses to identify trends and highlights that green finance can be linked to corporate performance through ESG variables [N5-F3]. In other words, studies often operationalize sustainability through composite indicators that combine environmental, social, and governance dimensions, and through proxies such as carbon emissions, renewable energy, and fintech-related activity [N2-R4][N5-R2][N5-F3]. The evidence therefore suggests that fintech-sustainability studies rely on mixed measures that align with SDG targets but are often proxied by narrower financial and environmental variables.

Researchers capture household and individual access to financial services using account ownership, access to payments services, and broader financial inclusion indicators. The World Bank source states that access to affordable financial services such as payments, credit, savings products, and insurance is critical for poverty reduction and economic growth, and that access is measured by indicators such as the number of bank branches and ATMs, as well as internet and mobile phone availability [N1-F1]. The IMF working paper on digital financial inclusion similarly notes that access is captured by indicators related to availability of means to access payments services, including bank branches, ATMs, and internet/mobile phone accessibility [N3-F4]. This indicates that access is often operationalized through ownership and infrastructure availability rather than abstract eligibility.

Usage and transaction behavior are captured by account ownership, making/receiving payments, transaction volume, and digital financial services (DFS) usage. The IMF evidence explicitly states that usage focuses on demand-side elements such as account ownership and making/receiving payments through these accounts [N3-F4]. The Global Findex Database and fintech-specific evidence also emphasize transaction volume and mobile money usage as important variables, with mobile money accounts and daily transaction volumes used to measure digital financial inclusion [N6-R1][N6-R3][N3-R5]. In other words, usage is not only about having an account but also about actually using the service for payments, savings, and other transactions.

Researchers operationalize inclusion outcomes such as exclusion, savings, credit, and insurance through composite and demand-side measures. The World Bank evidence states that mere bank account ownership does not fulfill the objective of financial inclusion, implying that exclusion is measured by the gap between access and actual usage [N1-R2]. The IMF working paper notes that financial inclusion is measured by combining access and usage indicators into a composite index, and that the study constructs separate indices for traditional and digital financial inclusion before aggregating them into an overall measure [N3-F4]. The same source also explicitly mentions credit and savings as part of financial inclusion, even though the evidence indicates that the index is limited to payments and does not include all financial services [N3-F4]. This suggests that studies often operationalize inclusion outcomes through composite indicators that combine access, usage, and specific service outcomes, while explicitly acknowledging limitations when broader financial services are not fully measurable.

Fintech-specific adoption metrics are used alongside or instead of general financial inclusion indicators. The IMF evidence shows that fintech-specific metrics such as mobile money accounts, financial transactions, and digital payment data are used to measure digital financial inclusion and that fintech is increasingly seen as a driver of financial inclusion [N3-F4][N3-R1][N3-R5]. The Findex-related evidence also emphasizes that fintech adoption is measured through mobile money and digital payments, while the World Bank source notes that digital financial services are lowering costs, increasing speed, and enabling access for underserved sections [N1-F1][N6-R2][N6-R3]. This indicates that fintech-specific variables are increasingly used as direct proxies for fintech impact, especially when traditional financial inclusion indicators are insufficient or when researchers want to isolate fintech effects.

## Integrated final answer: economic variables used to evaluate fintech on financial inclusion and sustainable development

Researchers evaluating the impact of fintech on **financial inclusion** and **sustainable development** rely on a broad set of economic variables that span access, usage, outcome measures, methodological controls, and sustainability proxies. The evidence across the branch reports shows that these studies do not treat fintech as a single uniform effect; instead, they distinguish fintech adoption from broader financial-sector change, control for omitted factors, and operationalize outcomes through composite indicators and proxies.

---

## 1. Economic variables for financial inclusion

### Household and individual access to financial services
Researchers capture access to financial services using **account ownership**, **access to payments services**, and broader financial inclusion indicators. The World Bank source emphasizes that access to affordable financial services such as payments, credit, savings products, and insurance is critical for poverty reduction and economic growth [N1-F1]. The IMF working paper similarly states that access is captured by indicators related to availability of means to access payments services, including bank branches, ATMs, and internet/mobile phone accessibility [N3-F4]. This means that access is often operationalized through ownership and infrastructure availability, not just abstract eligibility.

### Usage and transaction behavior
Usage and transaction behavior are measured by **account ownership**, **making/receiving payments**, **transaction volume**, and **digital financial services (DFS) usage**. The IMF evidence explicitly notes that usage focuses on demand-side elements such as account ownership and making/receiving payments through these accounts [N3-F4]. The Findex-related evidence also emphasizes **mobile money accounts** and **digital payments** as important variables, with **transaction volume** used to measure digital financial inclusion [N6-R1][N6-R3][N3-R5]. In other words, usage is not only about having an account but also about actually using the service for payments, savings, and other transactions.

### Inclusion outcomes: exclusion, savings, credit, and insurance
Researchers operationalize inclusion outcomes such as **exclusion**, **savings**, **credit**, and **insurance** through composite and demand-side measures. The World Bank evidence states that mere bank account ownership does not fulfill the objective of financial inclusion, implying that **exclusion** is measured by the gap between access and actual usage [N1-R2]. The IMF working paper notes that financial inclusion is measured by combining access and usage indicators into a composite index, and that the study constructs separate indices for traditional and digital financial inclusion before aggregating them into an overall measure [N3-F4]. While the evidence indicates that the index is limited to payments and does not include all financial services, it still shows that studies often operationalize inclusion outcomes through composite indicators that combine access, usage, and specific service outcomes [N3-F4].

### Fintech-specific adoption metrics
Fintech-specific adoption metrics are used alongside or instead of general financial inclusion indicators. The IMF evidence shows that fintech-specific metrics such as **mobile money accounts**, **financial transactions**, and **digital payment data** are used to measure digital financial inclusion and that fintech is increasingly seen as a driver of financial inclusion [N3-F4][N3-R1][N3-R5]. The Findex-related evidence also emphasizes that fintech adoption is measured through **mobile money** and **digital payments**, while the World Bank source notes that digital financial services are lowering costs, increasing speed, and enabling access for underserved sections [N1-F1][N6-R2][N6-R3]. This indicates that fintech-specific variables are increasingly used as direct proxies for fintech impact, especially when traditional financial inclusion indicators are insufficient or when researchers want to isolate fintech effects.

## 2. Economic variables for sustainable development

### Poverty, employment, and living standards
Studies linking fintech to sustainable development typically use variables that measure **poverty**, **employment**, and **living standards**. The official UNDP source defines the SDGs as covering poverty eradication, hunger, health, education, gender equality, and environmental sustainability, and emphasizes that the goals are designed to end poverty, hunger, AIDS, and discrimination against women and girls through improved health, education, and reduced inequality [N2-R1][N2-R3]. The UNDP material also highlights that extreme poverty fell below 10 percent globally, but 736 million people still lived on less than $1.90 a day, and 1.3 billion lived in multidimensional poverty [N2-F2]. This suggests that poverty is measured through extreme poverty lines, multidimensional poverty, and access to basic needs, while living standards are measured through income, poverty reduction, and access to services.

### Education and health outcomes
Education and health outcomes are measured through proxies and SDG-aligned indicators. The evidence shows that studies use indicators such as **access to education**, **health services**, and **malnutrition** and **undernourishment** [N2-F2]. The UNDP source specifically highlights **Goal 2 Zero Hunger** and **Goal 3 Good Health and Well-being**, with undernourishment dropping by nearly half in the past two decades while 821 million people were still chronically undernourished in 2017 [N2-F2]. It also notes that severe food insecurity and underweight among children remain major concerns, with over 90 million children under five dangerously underweight [N2-F2]. Education outcomes are indirectly operationalized through broader SDG language and poverty reduction goals, though the evidence does not provide a detailed enumeration of education-specific variables beyond SDG-aligned terminology.

Environmental sustainability and green finance outcomes are measured through **carbon emissions**, **renewable energy**, **energy efficiency**, and **investment flows**. The green finance source states that green finance aligns financial flows with sustainability objectives by supporting investments in renewable energy, energy-efficient construction, and other environmentally advantageous activities [N5-R2]. It also notes that the study’s bibliometric analysis focuses on carbon emissions, renewable energy, green technology innovation, and fintech [N5-F3]. This indicates that environmental outcomes are often operationalized through proxies such as emissions, clean-energy investment, and innovation in green technology, rather than through a single direct environmental indicator.

### SDG-aligned metrics
SDG-aligned metrics are operationalized in studies linking fintech to sustainability through **composite indicators** and **proxy variables**. The green finance source emphasizes the need to harmonize financial strategies with sustainability objectives and to use **ESG-related variables** and performance indicators [N5-F3]. It also notes that the study uses PRISMA and bibliometric analyses to identify trends and highlights that green finance can be linked to corporate performance through ESG variables [N5-F3]. ## 3. Methodological variables and controls in fintech impact studies

Researchers distinguish fintech adoption from broader financial-sector change by focusing on **fintech-specific adoption metrics** rather than generic financial-sector growth or penetration indicators. The evidence shows that fintech studies use digital financial inclusion indices and fintech-enabled access measures to capture the unique contribution of fintech, such as **mobile money accounts**, **digital payments**, **app usage**, and **transaction volumes**, while broader financial inclusion indicators remain important for comparison [N3-F4][N3-R1][N3-R5]. This distinction is important because fintech adoption can be a subset of broader financial-sector transformation, and studies need to isolate fintech effects from other financial development or regulatory changes.

### Standard control variables in cross-country and panel studies
Standard control variables in cross-country and panel studies include **macroeconomic and institutional controls**. The econometric evidence points to **panel-data methods** and **instrumental variables (IV)** as key methodological tools, with IV used to address endogeneity and identification problems [N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-R5]. Although the evidence does not list every possible control variable, the methodological literature implies that researchers commonly include variables such as **GDP growth**, **inflation**, **interest rates**, **credit expansion**, and possibly **financial depth indicators** as standard controls.

### Addressing endogeneity and identification
Researchers address endogeneity and identification in fintech studies by using **instrumental variables** and **panel-data strategies**. The evidence explicitly identifies IV as a method for treatment assignment where the instrument influences fintech adoption but not the outcome directly, and it also references **double-filter instrumental variable estimation** in panel data models with weakly exogenous variables [N4-R3][N4-R5]. This suggests that identification strategies in fintech studies are often designed to separate adoption from outcome and to account for reverse causality or omitted-variable bias. The evidence also points to the use of observed measurements as proxies for unobserved factors, which helps mitigate identification problems when direct data on adoption drivers are limited [N4-R2][N4-R4].

### Proxies for omitted factors
Variables used to proxy for omitted factors include **institutional quality**, **regulatory environment**, and **technology readiness**. The econometric evidence mentions observed measurements as proxies for unobserved factors or loadings, which can include institutional quality, regulatory environment, and technology readiness [N4-R2][N4-R4]. The contextual material from the fintech and digital finance literature also implies that researchers use fintech-specific adoption metrics such as **mobile money accounts**, **financial transactions**, **app downloads**, and **transaction volumes** as proxies for technology readiness and adoption intensity [N3-R1][N3-R5]. Together, these controls and proxies help researchers distinguish fintech effects from broader financial-sector or macroeconomic changes.

---

## 4. Variables linking fintech to sustainable development outcomes

### Fintech variables linked to green finance and climate finance
The evidence shows that fintech variables linked to **green finance** and **climate finance** outcomes include **fintech penetration**, **green finance instruments**, and **fintech-enabled sustainability infrastructure**. The green finance source states that green finance aligns financial flows with sustainability objectives by supporting investments in renewable energy, energy-efficient construction, and other environmentally advantageous activities, and that fintech is included among the instruments and assets used to promote environmentally aware and ecologically sustainable enterprises [N5-R2][N5-F3]. It also notes that fintech is part of a broader **greentech transition**, suggesting that fintech adoption metrics such as **app usage**, **transaction volumes**, and **digital financial services** can serve as proxies for green finance readiness and climate finance engagement [N3-R1][N3-R5][N5-F3]. Additionally, the bibliometric analysis explicitly identifies **carbon emissions**, **renewable energy**, **green technology innovation**, and **fintech** as relevant variables in this literature [N5-F3].

### Economic variables capturing sustainability-related impacts
Economic variables that capture sustainability-related impacts include **emissions**, **energy efficiency**, **investment flows**, and broader macroeconomic indicators. The green finance source emphasizes **carbon emissions** and **renewable energy** as central sustainability variables, and it also notes that green finance can influence corporate performance through ESG variables [N5-R2][N5-F3]. The fintech and green finance source further links fintech to green finance and sustainable development through the SDGs, particularly **SDG 13 Climate Action** and **SDG 7 Affordable and Clean Energy** [N5-F3]. This implies that studies often use **emissions** and **energy efficiency** as direct economic sustainability indicators, while **investment flows** and macroeconomic indicators such as **financial depth** or **credit expansion** are used to capture the broader economic channels through which fintech affects sustainability.

### Operationalizing sustainability impact
Studies operationalize the sustainability impact of fintech through **proxies** and **composite indicators**. The evidence indicates that sustainability impacts are often operationalized through composite measures combining **environmental, social, and governance (ESG)** variables [N5-F3]. The green finance source also notes that the study’s bibliometric approach identifies the most significant authors, sources, and emerging research domains, and that it focuses on **carbon emissions**, **renewable energy**, **green technology innovation**, and **fintech** [N5-F3]. This suggests that fintech-sustainability studies use proxies such as **carbon emissions**, **renewable energy**, and fintech adoption metrics alongside composite indicators to measure sustainability impact. The broader SDG-aligned evidence reinforces that environmental sustainability is usually measured through a combination of **emissions**, **clean energy**, and related financial flows, rather than through a single direct measure [N2-F2][N5-R2].

---

## 5. Bottom line

Overall, researchers evaluating the impact of fintech on **financial inclusion** and **sustainable development** use a layered set of economic variables:

- **For financial inclusion**: account ownership, access to payments services, usage and transaction behavior, and fintech-specific adoption metrics such as mobile money accounts, digital payments, app downloads, and transaction volume [N1-F1][N3-F4][N6-R1][N6-R3][N3-R5].
- **For sustainable development**: poverty, employment, living standards, education and health outcomes, carbon emissions, renewable energy, energy efficiency, investment flows, and SDG-aligned composite indicators [N2-R1][N2-F2][N5-R2][N5-F3].
- **Methodologically**: panel-data methods, instrumental variables, control variables such as GDP growth and macroeconomic indicators, and proxies for institutional quality and technology readiness [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R5].
- **For fintech-sustainability links**: fintech penetration, green finance instruments, carbon emissions, renewable energy, and composite ESG or sustainability indicators [N5-R2][N5-F3][N3-R1][N3-R5].

These variables are not used in isolation. Instead, studies often combine them into **composite indices**, **proxy measures**, and **SDG-aligned frameworks** to evaluate whether fintech expands access to financial services and whether it contributes to broader sustainability objectives [N3-F4][N5-F3][N2-F2].

## 1. Economic variables for financial inclusion

### Household and individual access to financial services
Researchers capture access to financial services using **account ownership**, **access to payments services**, and broader financial inclusion indicators. The World Bank source emphasizes that access to affordable financial services such as payments, credit, savings products, and insurance is critical for poverty reduction and economic growth [N1-F1]. The IMF working paper similarly states that access is captured by indicators related to availability of means to access payments services, including bank branches, ATMs, and internet/mobile phone accessibility [N3-F4]. This means that access is often operationalized through ownership and infrastructure availability, not just abstract eligibility.

### Usage and transaction behavior
Usage and transaction behavior are measured by **account ownership**, **making/receiving payments**, **transaction volume**, and **digital financial services (DFS) usage**. The IMF evidence explicitly notes that usage focuses on demand-side elements such as account ownership and making/receiving payments through these accounts [N3-F4]. The Findex-related evidence also emphasizes **mobile money accounts** and **digital payments** as important variables, with **transaction volume** used to measure digital financial inclusion [N6-R1][N6-R3][N3-R5]. In other words, usage is not only about having an account but also about actually using the service for payments, savings, and other transactions.

### Inclusion outcomes: exclusion, savings, credit, and insurance
Researchers operationalize inclusion outcomes such as **exclusion**, **savings**, **credit**, and **insurance** through composite and demand-side measures. The World Bank evidence states that mere bank account ownership does not fulfill the objective of financial inclusion, implying that **exclusion** is measured by the gap between access and actual usage [N1-R2]. The IMF working paper notes that financial inclusion is measured by combining access and usage indicators into a composite index, and that the study constructs separate indices for traditional and digital financial inclusion before aggregating them into an overall measure [N3-F4]. While the evidence indicates that the index is limited to payments and does not include all financial services, it still shows that studies often operationalize inclusion outcomes through composite indicators that combine access, usage, and specific service outcomes [N3-F4].

Fintech-specific adoption metrics are used alongside or instead of general financial inclusion indicators. The IMF evidence shows that fintech-specific metrics such as **mobile money accounts**, **financial transactions**, and **digital payment data** are used to measure digital financial inclusion and that fintech is increasingly seen as a driver of financial inclusion [N3-F4][N3-R1][N3-R5]. The Findex-related evidence also emphasizes that fintech adoption is measured through **mobile money** and **digital payments**, while the World Bank source notes that digital financial services are lowering costs, increasing speed, and enabling access for underserved sections [N1-F1][N6-R2][N6-R3]. This indicates that fintech-specific variables are increasingly used as direct proxies for fintech impact, especially when traditional financial inclusion indicators are insufficient or when researchers want to isolate fintech effects.
